description_full: Century Communities, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the design, development, construction, marketing, and sale of single-family attached and detached homes. It is also involved in the entitlement and development of the underlying land; and provision of mortgage, title, and insurance services to its homebuyers. The company offers homes under the Century Communities and Century Complete brands. It sells homes through its sales representatives, retail studios, and internet, as well as through independent real estate brokers in 18 states in the United States. Century Communities, Inc. was founded in 2002 and is headquartered in Greenwood Village, Colorado.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $2.5M ranks in the above the sector median among Real Estate peers, with revenue growing 25%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $75K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $12K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: Century Communities, Inc. is a small-cap real estate business with a $1.5B market cap on $4.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +19% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 17% against a 10% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $124M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.04× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 3.4×.

Management returns a meaningful 11.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 14% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
